Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel on 2 April 2026 — a suspect was arrested, a positive institutional response. Two additional deaths in April 2026, one of them a gay man, were linked by the top government lawyer's office to organised crime. An NGO observatory report counted 46 LGBT+ homicides in this state/province between 2015 and 2024, led by the main city (11), then a second city (6), two more (5 each) and a fourth (4), with 2015 the deadliest year (10 victims).

A local LGBT+ collective reports rising attacks in the municipalities bordering a neighbouring state/province, that victims are no longer attended to, and that the state/province does not acknowledge the violence. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol — the only counterweights are individual arrests.

Context for comparison: another state/province, similarly hostile, at least passed a gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025; the capital pairs comparable lethality with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocols. This state/province has no legal machinery whatsoever, plus an armed-group amplifier that makes the violence harder to escape or report.

This state/province recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. The national capital is the seat of the national protective apparatus and of the offices of human-rights bodies; a trans-rights organisation's own annual report is compiled and reported from this state/province's desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with another major city (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, this state/province's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against a population of several million give a rate of ~0.67 per million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.

The country's national protections and functioning rule of law apply unchanged here; the documented counter-action was policed without event cancellation or reported injuries. Earlier assertions of a wider multi-city attack pattern lack support in the retained sources and are removed from the record.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province carried a state/province-level anti-LGBT resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under pressure from the regional funding authority. Its municipality of tens of thousands of residents was the first local authority in the whole country to adopt such a resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to the capital's LGBT+ Declaration signed a month earlier. The municipality became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other state/provinces the repeal was coerced rather than converted—the underlying civic mobilisation that produced the country's first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the state/province scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Score of 0.45 sits 0.07 below the national 0.52. Above one state/province (0.42), which additionally produced a mayoral march ban and held out until 2025, and above another (0.44), where the 2019 coordinated mass assault adds a violence dimension absent here. Below a third (0.48), which pairs its resolution history with a clearly positive institutional trajectory in its main city.
rewrites.blindTangential: The resolution history targeted 'LGBT ideology' broadly rather than trans status specifically; with the document repealed, no formal instrument remains, but the mobilisation that produced the country's first anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto general-hostility signal.
blindSourceSummaries: A scholarly analysis (8 April 2020): a town in this state/province became the country's first anti-LGBT zone when its local council passed a non-binding resolution in March 2019 pledging to protect children from 'homosexual propaganda' and to refrain from actions encouraging 'tolerance of LGBT people'. Scholarly framing of the record's first-in-country claim, plus the resolution's embedding in global anti-gender campaigning.

A news outlet (23 September 2021, updated 29 September): on Monday 20 September 2021 three state/provinces repealed their anti-LGBT resolutions — this state/province notable because it had previously voted to keep its resolution, and all the repeals followed the regional funding authority's funding threats. Confirms the record's repeal date of 20 September 2021 under pressure from the regional funding authority.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province was one of the five state/provinces that formally adopted an "anti-LGBT ideology" resolution by mid-2020, placing approximately one-third of the country under declarations whose stated purpose was to exclude LGBTQ public events. It sits in the governing party's heartland belt. The resolution was struck down or repealed in the 2021 wave following the regional funding authority's funding threats.

No march ban, coordinated attack, or county-level holdout comparable to other state/provinces' documented cases is recorded for this state/province. The sub-national finding is the regional resolution itself and its location in the conservative bloc; the practical visitor-facing exposure is the general social climate of that bloc rather than a specific enforcement or violence event.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52, matching another state/province (0.48) for having a state/province-level resolution without an additional capital-city positive counterweight or a documented enforcement/violence episode. Well above two other state/provinces (0.42 and 0.44), both of which carry specific ban or assault evidence.
rewrites.blindTangential: The state/province resolution was an anti-LGBT-ideology declaration (LGBT broadly, not trans-specific) and is formally gone; the visitor-facing residue is the conservative bloc's general civic climate rather than any enforcement or violence event documented for this unit.
blindSourceSummaries: Per-state/province revocation record: the country's top administrative court revoked this state/province's anti-LGBT resolution on 12 October 2023, and another state/province's council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021 (the regional funding authority had written to the heads of five state/provinces on 2 June 2020 about the resolutions). By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all local government family-rights charters in the country had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 local governments in this country adopted 'anti-LGBT zone'-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area; the country's administrative courts struck them down as unconstitutional (equal-treatment guarantee), the regional funding authority linked development funds to their repeal, and the last remaining zone was abolished in 2025. The article notes the resolutions were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal — they created no new penalties and barred no one physically — but signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate.
